question: On four named binary tabular datasets (OpenML adult v2 [data_id 1590], bank-marketing [1461], electricity [151] and phoneme [1489], each capped at a stratified sample of at most 20,000 rows, with a calibration-split fraction fixed at the design gate so that every calibration split has at least 1,000 cases), how well calibrated are the predicted probabilities of logistic regression, random forests and gradient-boosted trees with library defaults (scikit-learn 1.9.1, no tuning), and how do Platt scaling and isotonic regression fitted on a held-out calibration split change log-loss, Brier score and calibration error, with the base model held fixed?
hypotheses: H1 (a test, on the plug-in ECE estimator, of the direction Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana 2005 reported; never called a replication; the debiased ECE is reported descriptively): without recalibration, random forests have higher expected calibration error than logistic regression as measured by the plug-in binned estimator (15 equal-mass bins on P(y=1), sum over bins of bin share times |mean label - mean prediction|; tie handling at bin edges fixed in design.method step 8). This estimator is biased upward, and its bias is not additive: for a well-calibrated model it sits at a noise floor of about 0.8 x sqrt(p(1-p)/n_b) per bin (roughly 0.01-0.02 at 5,000 test rows, 0.03-0.04 at phoneme's 1,351), while for a clearly miscalibrated model it shrinks toward zero as the true gap grows. So if RF is miscalibrated and LR well calibrated, the RF-minus-LR difference is pulled toward zero (against H1) by up to LR's floor; if both are well calibrated, it equals the difference of their floors, whose sign depends on how each model spreads its predictions. The H1 verdict is therefore a statement about this estimator on these samples, not about the population calibration error; the debiased estimator of Kumar et al. (2019) is reported beside it descriptively and never changes the verdict; it removes only about 41% of a well-calibrated bin's floor, so its agreement does not show that a verdict is free of a floor artefact. Brier and log-loss are reported descriptively; Fonseca and Lopes (2017) report that on Brier score uncalibrated random forests often beat logistic regression. Decision rule per dataset (fixed now): for each of 10 seeds, the difference (treatment minus comparison) is taken on the same seed, subsample and splits (for H1, random forest minus logistic regression; for H2, isotonic minus no recalibration on the same fitted model). The 95% interval is a plain paired t(9) interval over those 10 differences on every dataset. Because seeds resample overlapping rows of the same pool, this interval measures variability over resplits of these samples, not population sampling variance, and the verdicts are scoped to these samples. Categories, in order of precedence: (1) 'no difference' if the whole interval lies within +/- the margin (Brier 0.001; ECE 0.005); (2) 'holds' if the whole interval lies on the predicted side; (3) 'contradicted' if it lies wholly on the other side; (4) otherwise 'no detectable difference (inconclusive)'. Overall: supported if it holds on at least 3 of the 4 datasets and is contradicted on none; contradicted if contradicted on at least 2; 'no difference' if 'no difference' on at least 3 and holds or is contradicted on none; otherwise inconclusive. All verdicts are scoped to these samples.

H2a (contested in prior work): isotonic regression fitted on the held-out split lowers the Brier score of random forests relative to no recalibration. Log-loss (with a clipping epsilon fixed at the design gate, clip counts reported) and ECE are reported descriptively. Decision rule per dataset (fixed now): for each of 10 seeds, the difference (treatment minus comparison) is taken on the same seed, subsample and splits (for H1, random forest minus logistic regression; for H2, isotonic minus no recalibration on the same fitted model). The 95% interval is a plain paired t(9) interval over those 10 differences on every dataset. Because seeds resample overlapping rows of the same pool, this interval measures variability over resplits of these samples, not population sampling variance, and the verdicts are scoped to these samples. Categories, in order of precedence: (1) 'no difference' if the whole interval lies within +/- the margin (Brier 0.001; ECE 0.005); (2) 'holds' if the whole interval lies on the predicted side; (3) 'contradicted' if it lies wholly on the other side; (4) otherwise 'no detectable difference (inconclusive)'. Overall: supported if it holds on at least 3 of the 4 datasets and is contradicted on none; contradicted if contradicted on at least 2; 'no difference' if 'no difference' on at least 3 and holds or is contradicted on none; otherwise inconclusive. All verdicts are scoped to these samples.

H2b (an extension of Fonseca and Lopes 2017): isotonic regression lowers the Brier score of scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier relative to no recalibration. Log-loss and ECE are reported descriptively. Decision rule per dataset (fixed now): for each of 10 seeds, the difference (treatment minus comparison) is taken on the same seed, subsample and splits (for H1, random forest minus logistic regression; for H2, isotonic minus no recalibration on the same fitted model). The 95% interval is a plain paired t(9) interval over those 10 differences on every dataset. Because seeds resample overlapping rows of the same pool, this interval measures variability over resplits of these samples, not population sampling variance, and the verdicts are scoped to these samples. Categories, in order of precedence: (1) 'no difference' if the whole interval lies within +/- the margin (Brier 0.001; ECE 0.005); (2) 'holds' if the whole interval lies on the predicted side; (3) 'contradicted' if it lies wholly on the other side; (4) otherwise 'no detectable difference (inconclusive)'. Overall: supported if it holds on at least 3 of the 4 datasets and is contradicted on none; contradicted if contradicted on at least 2; 'no difference' if 'no difference' on at least 3 and holds or is contradicted on none; otherwise inconclusive. All verdicts are scoped to these samples.
Platt scaling is applied to the logit of each model's predicted probability (one input scale for all models) and reported descriptively against none and isotonic; it is not a tested hypothesis.
contribution: Seed-resolved, per-model and per-dataset evidence on four named datasets, with the base model held fixed across recalibration methods with one confirmatory metric per hypothesis (ECE for H1, Brier score for H2a and H2b); a test, on the plug-in ECE estimator, of the direction of a known calibration result (H1; not a replication, with the debiased ECE of Kumar et al. 2019 reported descriptively); and an extension of earlier evidence on isotonic recalibration for random forests and modern gradient boosting. It does not settle the disagreement among larger benchmarks.

design.summary: For each of 10 seeds and each of four OpenML datasets (adult 1590, bank-marketing 1461, electricity 151, phoneme 1489), a stratified subsample of at most 20,000 rows is redrawn per seed and split 50/25/25 into train/calibration/test (calibration n = 5,000, or 1,351 on phoneme), one shared train-fitted preprocessing (median-impute and standardise numerics, one-hot categoricals) feeds scikit-learn 1.9.1 default logistic regression (max_iter=1000), random forest and HistGradientBoosting (early_stopping=False, which equals the 'auto' default at 10,000 training rows), each fitted once and frozen. Platt scaling and isotonic regression are fitted on the calibration split through FrozenEstimator on the logit of the probability clipped to [1e-6, 1-1e-6], and every (dataset, model, calibrator, seed) is scored once on the test split for Brier score, log-loss (eps 1e-6, clip counts), 15-bin equal-mass ECE on P(y=1) with tied predictions never split across bins, the debiased ECE of Kumar et al. (2019), and ROC-AUC. H1 (ECE, RF minus LR, no recalibration), H2a (Brier, RF isotonic minus none) and H2b (Brier, HGB isotonic minus none) are decided exactly by the pre-registered paired t(9) rule with margins 0.005 (ECE) and 0.001 (Brier) and the k-of-4 overall rule; sensitivity runs (Kumar et al.'s debiased ECE for H1, isotonic on 1,351 calibration rows for H2, a chronological split on electricity) are reported but never change a verdict, and the whole plan costs about 4 CPU-minutes on synthetic data of the same shapes (budget cap 60 CPU-minutes).
design.method:
EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE (fixed before any run on study data; any departure is logged with crew.py log and disclosed in the paper).

1. Datasets and labels. adult (OpenML data_id 1590), bank-marketing (1461), electricity (151), phoneme (1489), as pinned by the Data RA in data/manifest.json (version, file id, sha256) and described in data/CODEBOOK.md. Dataset index d: adult=0, bank-marketing=1, electricity=2, phoneme=3. y=1 is the label recorded in data/manifest.json target_encoding (confirmed: adult '>50K', bank-marketing '2' = subscribed a term deposit, electricity 'UP', phoneme '2' = oral vowel); data/raw/<name>.csv already carries it as the integer column 'target'. The experiment reads each dataset's numeric_features, categorical_features and target from data/manifest.json, never from CSV dtypes (LIAC-ARFF writes integer-valued numerics as floats, and electricity's day levels 1-7 or bank-marketing's codes would otherwise be inferred as numbers); categorical columns are read as strings with empty cells as missing, numeric columns as float64, and the code asserts that the CSV header equals the manifest's numeric_features and categorical_features (in OpenML column order) plus 'target'. Brier, log-loss and AUC are invariant to which label is 1; ECE is computed on P(y=1) under the tie rule in step 8. Features are used exactly as the loader returns them (adult keeps fnlwgt and both education columns; bank-marketing keeps the call-duration column V12; electricity keeps date, period and the Victoria columns including their constant fill values); no row is dropped. Row counts equal the OpenML metadata (48,842 / 45,211 / 45,312 / 5,404; checked by fetch-data); the experiment asserts them and the manifest sha256 of each CSV, and stops on a mismatch.

2. Seeds and random streams. Seeds s = 0..9. For each (d, s): ss = numpy.random.SeedSequence([20261119, d, s]); (sub, split, model, debias) = ss.spawn(4). Integers passed to scikit-learn: int(sub.generate_state(1)[0]) for the subsample; (i_test, i_cal) = split.generate_state(2) for the two splits; rs = int(model.generate_state(1)[0]) as random_state for RF and HGB and for the n_cal sensitivity subset; debias.spawn(12) gives the fixed seeds for the normal draws of the debiased ECE: children j = 0..8 for (model, calibrator) in the order (lr, rf, hgb) x (none, platt, isotonic) in main, and j = 9, 10, 11 for (lr, rf, hgb) with isotonic on the 1,351-row subset in sens-ncal; each is used as numpy.random.default_rng(child). sens-elec-time uses the same scheme with ss = numpy.random.SeedSequence([20261119, 2, s, 1]) (the fourth entry marks the chronological variant), whose split child is unused because the split is chronological. Within a (d, s), the subsample, splits, preprocessing and test rows are identical for all models and calibrators, so every comparison is paired by seed; the seed redraws the subsample, both splits and the models' random_state.

3. Subsample (redrawn per seed). If n > 20,000: sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split(X, y, train_size=20000, stratify=y, random_state=sub_int); otherwise (phoneme, 5,404 rows) all rows are used and only the splits change across seeds. Subsamples of different seeds overlap (about 44% of rows for two 20,000-row draws from about 45,000), which is why the interval in step 10 is scoped to these samples.

4. Split, 50/25/25, stratified on y. n_test = n_cal = round(0.25 n) as integers; test = train_test_split(test_size=n_test, stratify=y, random_state=i_test); calibration = train_test_split(rest, test_size=n_cal, stratify=y_rest, random_state=i_cal); train = the remainder. Sizes: 10,000 / 5,000 / 5,000 on adult, bank-marketing and electricity; 2,702 / 1,351 / 1,351 on phoneme. The code asserts n_cal >= 1,000 and n_train <= 10,000 in every cell and records n_train, n_cal, n_test and the positive count in each split.

5. Preprocessing ('library defaults' made exact). One sklearn ColumnTransformer, fitted on the training split's features only, applied unchanged to the calibration and test splits and shared by all three models. Numeric columns: SimpleImputer(strategy='median') then StandardScaler() (a no-op for tree partitions; the imputer is a no-op unless the CODEBOOK reports numeric missing values). Categorical columns = the manifest's categorical_features (adult: workclass, education, marital-status, occupation, relationship, race, sex, native-country; bank-marketing: V2, V3, V4, V5, V7, V8, V9, V11, V16; electricity: day; phoneme: none); every other feature is numeric: SimpleImputer(strategy='constant', fill_value='missing') then OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore', sparse_output=False). Output is a dense float64 array, so HistGradientBoosting's default categorical_features='from_dtype' treats every column as numeric (the code asserts is_categorical_ is None); HGB's native categorical handling is not used, so that all three models see identical inputs. Expected widths after encoding: about 108 (adult), 51 (bank-marketing), 14 (electricity: 7 numeric + 7 day levels), 5 (phoneme); the realised width is recorded.

6. Base models (scikit-learn 1.9.1, no tuning), each fitted once per (d, s) on the training split:
 - LR: LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), otherwise defaults (L2, C=1.0, lbfgs, tol=1e-4). max_iter=1000 is the only departure from defaults, to let lbfgs converge on one-hot inputs; n_iter_ and any ConvergenceWarning are recorded per cell and a non-converged cell is reported, not refitted.
 - RF: RandomForestClassifier(random_state=rs, n_jobs=1), otherwise defaults (100 trees, max_features='sqrt', min_samples_leaf=1, bootstrap=True).
 - HGB: HistGradientBoostingClassifier(early_stopping=False, random_state=rs), otherwise defaults (log_loss, learning_rate=0.1, max_iter=100, max_leaf_nodes=31, min_samples_leaf=20, max_bins=255). The 'auto' default switches early stopping on only when the training sample exceeds 10,000 rows (gradient_boosting.py line 534: n_samples > 10_000); with n_train = 10,000 or 2,702 it is off on every dataset, so early_stopping=False reproduces the default exactly and makes the procedure identical by construction (the code asserts n_iter_ == 100).
 Worker processes run with threadpoolctl limits of 1 thread, so results do not depend on thread scheduling.

7. Calibrators, with the base model frozen. Each fitted base model is wrapped in LogitScore, a fitted classifier whose decision_function(X) = logit(clip(predict_proba(X)[:,1], 1e-6, 1-1e-6)), with predict and predict_proba delegated. Then CalibratedClassifierCV(FrozenEstimator(LogitScore(base)), method=m, ensemble=False).fit(X_cal, y_cal) for m in {'sigmoid', 'isotonic'}. With a FrozenEstimator the base model is never refitted; ensemble=False fits one calibrator on all calibration rows (the cross_val_predict call returns the frozen model's own scores). 'sigmoid' is scikit-learn's Platt fit (Platt's smoothed targets, L-BFGS-B, no regularisation) on the logit, the same input scale for all three models; 'isotonic' is IsotonicRegression(out_of_bounds='clip') on the same scores. It equals isotonic regression on the clipped probability only at the calibration points; between them scikit-learn interpolates linearly in the logit, not in the probability (max |difference| on synthetic models about 0.001; code-r1 F3), so the paper describes the calibrator as isotonic regression fitted on the logit score with linear interpolation in the logit. 'none' is base.predict_proba(X_test)[:,1]. The code asserts that the base model's test probabilities are bit-identical before and after both calibrator fits. The calibration split is used for nothing else, and nothing is tuned on it or on the test split.

8. Metrics, computed once per (dataset, model, calibrator, seed) on the test split from p = P(y=1) (4 x 3 x 3 x 10 = 360 rows):
 - brier = mean((p - y)^2), unclipped (asserted equal to sklearn.metrics.brier_score_loss).
 - logloss = -mean(y log pc + (1-y) log(1-pc)), pc = clip(p, 1e-6, 1-1e-6); n_clip_low = #{p < 1e-6}, n_clip_high = #{p > 1-1e-6} recorded per row. logloss_mach (pc clipped at float64 machine epsilon 2.22e-16, what sklearn.metrics.log_loss does in 1.9.1) is reported as a descriptive sensitivity.
 - ece = sum over bins b of (n_b/n) |mean(y in b) - mean(p in b)|, 15 equal-mass bins on P(y=1). Tie rule: with q = round(p, 12), each prediction goes to bin floor(15 * #{j: q_j < q_i} / n), so a group of tied predictions is never split across bins and sits in the bin where its first member would fall; bins left empty are dropped. The estimator depends only on the multiset of (p, y), not on row order. ece_bins = number of non-empty bins is recorded.
 - ece_db = the debiased estimator for the binned l1 calibration error of Kumar, Liang and Ma (2019), Appendix G, Definition G.3 (arXiv:1909.10155v2), on the same 15 bins and tie rule as ece. For each non-empty bin k with n_k predictions: p_k = n_k/n, y_k = mean label, s_k = mean prediction (so ece = sum_k p_k |s_k - y_k|, their Definition G.2). Draw R_k^(m) ~ Normal(y_k, y_k(1-y_k)/n_k) for m = 1..M with M = 1,000 (PI ruling), as one call rng.normal(loc=y, scale=sqrt(y(1-y)/n_k), size=(1000, K)) over the K non-empty bins in increasing bin order, where rng is the fixed-seed Generator of step 2 for that (dataset, seed, model, calibrator), so ece_db is reproducible exactly; then ece_db = ece - (mean_m sum_k p_k |s_k - R_k^(m)| - ece) = 2*ece - mean_m sum_k p_k |s_k - R_k^(m)|. A bin with y_k in {0, 1} has zero variance and contributes no correction. ece_db can be negative and is reported as it is, never floored at 0: a negative value means the plug-in ECE lies within its own sampling noise of zero, and flooring would reintroduce an upward bias and distort the seed means and paired differences that sensitivity (a) averages. It removes only part of the plug-in bias (code-r1 F2): for a well-calibrated bin with s_k - y_k ~ Normal(0, sigma^2), E|s_k - y_k| = sigma sqrt(2/pi) while the simulated term E|s_k - R_k| = sqrt(2) sigma sqrt(2/pi), so E[ece_db] = (2 - sqrt(2)) sigma sqrt(2/pi), about 0.59 of the plug-in floor; it removes only about 41% (1 - (2 - sqrt 2)) of a calibrated bin's l1 floor (unit-tests measured a remaining 0.56) and close to none for a clearly miscalibrated bin. A pure floor difference between two models therefore reappears in ece_db at about 0.6 times its size with the same sign, and agreement between ece_db and the plug-in verdict is not evidence that the H1 verdict is free of a floor artefact; Kumar et al. call it a heuristic: their guarantees cover the squared (l2) calibration error, not the unsquared ECE, and the paper presents ece_db as a heuristic without such a guarantee (claims c-kumar-debiased-ece, c-kumar-heuristic). The source says only 'many draws'; M = 1,000 was fixed by the PI. Descriptive sensitivity for H1 only.
 - auc = sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score(y, p): control for discrimination lost through isotonic ties (Platt is strictly monotone and keeps AUC).
 - bookkeeping: n_train, n_cal, n_test, positives per split, encoded width, lr_n_iter, lr_converged, hgb_n_iter, fit seconds (not compared on rerun).
 Test labels and probabilities for every (d, s, model, calibrator) are saved with numpy.savez_compressed, one .npz per (dataset, seed) and run (results/preds/<run>/<dataset>_s<seed>.npz, float64 arrays y and p_<model>_<calibrator>), for the reliability figures. results/preds/ is git-ignored and rebuilt by rerunning the run, like data/raw/.

9. Hypothesis differences, paired by seed (d_s = treatment_s - comparison_s on the same seed, subsample and splits):
 - H1: d_s = ece(RF, none, s) - ece(LR, none, s); predicted side d > 0; margin 0.005.
 - H2a: d_s = brier(RF, isotonic, s) - brier(RF, none, s); predicted side d < 0; margin 0.001.
 - H2b: d_s = brier(HGB, isotonic, s) - brier(HGB, none, s); predicted side d < 0; margin 0.001.

10. Decision rule (as stated in plan.json hypotheses; computed in code/analyze.py). Per dataset: mean dbar, sample SD sd (ddof=1), CI = dbar -/+ t_{0.975, 9} * sd / sqrt(10), t_{0.975, 9} = 2.2621571628 (scipy.stats.t.ppf). Categories in order of precedence: (1) 'no difference' if -margin <= lo and hi <= margin; (2) 'holds' if the interval lies wholly on the predicted side (lo > 0 for H1; hi < 0 for H2a/H2b); (3) 'contradicted' if it lies wholly on the other side (hi < 0 for H1; lo > 0 for H2a/H2b); (4) otherwise 'no detectable difference (inconclusive)'. Overall, over the four datasets: 'supported' if holds on >= 3 and contradicted on none; 'contradicted' if contradicted on >= 2; 'no difference' if 'no difference' on >= 3 and holds or contradicted on none; otherwise 'inconclusive' (the first three are mutually exclusive). The interval measures variability over resplits of these samples, not population sampling variance, and every verdict is scoped to these samples. No correction for the three hypotheses x four datasets; the k-of-4 rule is the only aggregation.

11. Descriptive comparisons (no verdict): Platt minus none and isotonic minus Platt for every model and dataset on Brier, log-loss, ECE and AUC; H1 on Brier and log-loss (Fonseca and Lopes 2017 report RF often beats LR on Brier); mean and SD over the 10 seeds for every (dataset, model, calibrator) and metric; paired t(9) intervals shown for these but labelled descriptive. Sensitivities (step 12) are reported beside the confirmatory verdicts; where they disagree, the paper and abstract state the confirmatory verdict and the disagreement together, and the confirmatory metric is never swapped after results.

12. Sensitivity runs (pre-declared, verdict-neutral): (a) H1 recomputed on ece_db with the same paired t(9) rule and margin, reported only and never changing the H1 verdict (estimator bias of plug-in ECE); (b) sens-ncal: on adult, bank-marketing and electricity, isotonic refitted on a stratified 1,351-row subset of each seed's calibration split (train_test_split(train_size=1351, stratify, random_state=rs)) with the same frozen base model and test split, and H2a/H2b categories recomputed, so that calibration n equals phoneme's on all four datasets. This equalises calibration n only: phoneme still differs in training n (2,702 vs 10,000, so a different base model) and test n (1,351 vs 5,000, so noisier scores), so a phoneme-specific H2 pattern that survives sens-ncal is not thereby attributed to the dataset; (c) sens-elec-time: on electricity only, each seed's 20,000-row subsample is sorted by original file row index and split chronologically 50/25/25 (fetch-data established that file row order is time order: 944 whole days x 48 half-hours, day index = row // 48, half-hour = row % 48; the normalised date column drops five times in file order and is not used for ordering; for electricity, in main and in sens-elec-time, the number of rows taken from the first 17,424 file rows (constant Victoria fill values) in each of train, calibration and test is recorded per seed) (earliest half train, next quarter calibration, latest quarter test), all three models refitted with the same settings, and H1/H2a/H2b differences and categories reported for electricity only, never counted in the k-of-4.

13. Code review before any analysis run. code/experiment.py, code/analyze.py, code/describe.py, the two sensitivity scripts and code/test_metrics.py are reviewed by the Reviewer (target 'code') against this method after the design gate and before main runs; test_metrics.py (a data-prep run on hand-made and synthetic inputs only) checks the ECE tie rule on hand-computed cases, the clip counts, brier against sklearn, LogitScore against the base model's probabilities, and that FrozenEstimator leaves the base model unchanged. No study data is scored before the code review passes with no open critical finding.

14. Compute. Timing run timing-synthetic (data-prep, code/timing_synthetic.py) ran the per-cell procedure, including both sensitivities and a plug-in ECE null floor of 200 Bernoulli resamples of all test rows per (model, calibrator) that the design-r1 revision replaced with ece_db (1,000 normal draws over at most 15 bins, about 15,000 numbers against about 1,000,000 for the floor on a 5,000-row test split, so the timing is an upper bound for this step and was not rerun), on make_classification data with the four post-cap shapes (2 seeds x 4 datasets, 8 workers, Apple M3, 8 cores): about 7.0 s per adult cell, 6.0 bank-marketing, 8.6 electricity (with the chronological split), 1.4 phoneme, so about 3.8 CPU-minutes and under 1 wall-minute for all 40 cells. Real data may grow fully grown RF trees several times deeper; allowing a factor of 5 gives about 20 CPU-minutes and about 3 wall-minutes. Budget cap: 60 CPU-minutes for all analysis runs together; if main alone exceeds 30 CPU-minutes the Experimenter stops and tells the PI before running anything else.
design.data:
Four OpenML binary tabular datasets, fetched with sklearn.datasets.fetch_openml pinned by data_id and recorded by the Data RA in data/manifest.json (data_id, version, file id, md5/sha256, licence, retrieval date) and data/CODEBOOK.md (rows, feature types, missing values, positive share, target encoding, electricity's time columns). The design names the dataset; no run may use an unpinned version.
 - adult, OpenML 1590 (v2): 48,842 rows; 6 numeric and 8 categorical features (missing values in workclass, occupation and native-country, imputed as a 'missing' category); positive '>50K', 11,687 rows (23.9%). Stratified 20,000-row subsample per seed; split 10,000 / 5,000 / 5,000.
 - bank-marketing, OpenML 1461: 45,211 rows; 7 numeric and 9 categorical features ('unknown' kept as a level); positive Class '2' = subscribed, 5,289 rows (11.7%); categorical V2, V3, V4, V5, V7, V8, V9, V11, V16. 20,000 per seed; 10,000 / 5,000 / 5,000. The call-duration feature is kept as distributed (see threats).
 - electricity, OpenML 151 (Elec2, NSW market, half-hourly, 1996-1998): 45,312 rows; date, day (categorical, 7 levels), period, nswprice, nswdemand, vicprice, vicdemand, transfer; positive 'UP', 19,237 rows (42.5%). 20,000 per seed; 10,000 / 5,000 / 5,000. File row order is time order (944 days x 48 half-hours); the normalised date column is not monotone. vicprice, vicdemand and transfer are constant over the first 17,424 rows (363 days to early May 1997), fill values rather than measurements (threats; sens-elec-time).
 - phoneme, OpenML 1489: 5,404 rows; 5 numeric features; positive Class '2' = oral vowel, 1,586 rows (29.3%). All rows every seed; split 2,702 / 1,351 / 1,351.
Unit of observation: one row of the dataset. Unit of analysis: one (dataset, model, calibrator, seed) cell scored on its test split (360 cells); each hypothesis uses 10 paired per-seed differences per dataset. Row counts, positive labels and feature types above are as recorded by fetch-data in data/manifest.json and data/CODEBOOK.md (checked against OpenML qualities); the experiment reads feature lists and labels from the manifest (method step 1). Raw and derived data stay git-ignored and are rebuilt by the logged data-prep run.
analysis_plan: timing-synthetic (data-prep, designer; DONE 2026-11-19): code/timing_synthetic.py runs the per-cell procedure of design.method (subsample, 50/25/25 split, shared preprocessing, three default models, FrozenEstimator Platt and isotonic on the logit, all metrics including a plug-in ECE null floor (since replaced by the cheaper debiased ECE), the n_cal=1,351 isotonic sensitivity and the electricity chronological split) on make_classification pools with the four study shapes, 2 seeds x 4 datasets on 8 workers. It reads no study data and writes no score. Purpose: fix the compute budget. Result: about 3.8 CPU-minutes and under 1 wall-minute for all 40 cells.

fetch-data (data-prep, data-ra; DONE 2026-11-19): fetch and pin the four datasets (data/manifest.json, data/CODEBOOK.md, data/raw/<name>.csv). Purpose: fixed, versioned inputs and the positive-label and categorical-column lists the method reads. Must finish before main.

unit-tests (data-prep, experimenter): code/test_metrics.py on hand-made and synthetic inputs only: ECE tie rule against hand-computed cases (including a tie group spanning a bin edge and an all-tied vector), clip counts, brier equal to sklearn, LogitScore reproduces the base probabilities, FrozenEstimator leaves the base model's test probabilities bit-identical. Purpose: verify the metric code before any study data is scored.

code review (Reviewer, target 'code'): experiment.py, analyze.py, describe.py, sens_ncal.py, sens_elec_time.py and test_metrics.py checked against design.method after the design gate. Purpose: no analysis run before the review has no open critical finding.

main (analysis, experimenter): code/experiment.py writes results/cells.csv (360 rows: 4 datasets x 3 models x 3 calibrators x 10 seeds, all metrics of method step 8) and compressed .npz predictions under results/preds/main/ (git-ignored), with flat counts in runs/main/metrics.json. Purpose: the confirmatory data for H1, H2a and H2b.

h-tests (analysis, experimenter): code/analyze.py reads results/cells.csv and computes, for H1 (ECE), H2a and H2b (Brier), the per-dataset dbar, sd, 95% paired t(9) interval and category, and the overall verdict, exactly as method steps 9-10; also H1 on ece_db (Kumar et al. 2019 debiased ECE; sensitivity a), flagged as sensitivity and never changing the verdict. Metrics are flat (e.g. h1_adult_mean, h1_adult_lo, h1_adult_hi, h1_adult_cat; category codes 0 no difference, 1 holds, 2 contradicted, 3 inconclusive; h1_overall). Purpose: the verdicts.

describe (analysis, experimenter): code/describe.py: mean and SD over seeds for every (dataset, model, calibrator) on brier, logloss, logloss_mach, ece, ece_db, auc, clip counts, ece_bins; descriptive paired intervals for Platt minus none, isotonic minus Platt, and RF minus LR on Brier and log-loss; LR convergence and HGB n_iter checks. Purpose: everything the paper reports beside the verdicts, including the AUC control.

sens-ncal (analysis, experimenter): code/sens_ncal.py: isotonic refitted on a stratified 1,351-row subset of each seed's calibration split on adult, bank-marketing and electricity (same frozen base model and test split); H2a and H2b categories recomputed with phoneme's main cells. Purpose: show whether an H2 difference between phoneme and the other three datasets disappears when calibration n alone is equalised (it would then be consistent with a calibration-n effect). It does not equalise training n (2,702 vs 10,000) or test n (1,351 vs 5,000), so a pattern that survives is not attributed to the dataset itself.

sens-elec-time (analysis, experimenter): code/sens_elec_time.py: electricity only, each seed's subsample sorted by original file row index (the time order; not by date) and split chronologically 50/25/25, three models refitted, H1/H2a/H2b differences and categories for electricity reported, not counted in k-of-4. Purpose: show whether random-split temporal leakage drives the electricity results.

figures and tables (analysis, figures-ra): reliability diagrams (equal-mass bins, pooled over seeds) per dataset x model x calibrator from results/preds/, a forest plot of the per-dataset H1/H2a/H2b intervals with the margins, and the main table, all built from the run outputs. Purpose: the paper's figures, with no number typed by hand.
threats: Plug-in ECE is biased upward and its bias is not additive (design-r1 F1). For a well-calibrated model each bin's |mean label - mean prediction| has expectation about 0.8 x sqrt(p(1-p)/n_b): roughly 0.01-0.02 overall at 5,000 test rows (333 per bin) and 0.03-0.04 on phoneme (1,351 rows, 90 per bin), above H1's 0.005 margin. For a clearly miscalibrated model the bias shrinks toward zero. Hence if RF is miscalibrated and LR is not, RF minus LR is pulled toward zero, against H1, by up to LR's floor; if neither is, the difference equals the floor difference and can take either sign. H1's text was narrowed to this estimator (disclosed in plan.json disclosures). Only partly addressed. ece_db, the debiased l1 estimator of Kumar et al. (2019, Def. G.3), removes only about 41% (2 - sqrt 2 of the floor remains) of a well-calibrated bin's floor and close to none for a miscalibrated bin (code-r1 F2), so a floor difference between RF and LR reappears in ece_db at about 0.6 times its size with the same sign. H1 recomputed on ece_db (sensitivity a) is reported descriptively beside the confirmatory verdict and never changes it, and its agreement is not read as confirmation. ece_db is a heuristic without a guarantee for the unsquared ECE. The remedy is to narrow the claim: H1 is never called a replication; it is a test of the published direction on the plug-in estimator on these samples, and the paper states that its margin (0.005) is below the estimator's floor (about 0.01-0.04), so a verdict may reflect a difference in floors rather than in calibration.

Ties at equal-mass bin edges: RF outputs are near multiples of 0.01 and isotonic outputs are step functions, so bins cannot all be equal. Addressed by the fixed rule (ties never split; bin = floor(15 * #smaller / n)), which is independent of row order; ece_bins is reported per cell, and unit-tests checks the rule on hand-computed cases.

Calibration-set size, not model or dataset, may decide H2 (isotonic needs about 1,000+ cases; niculescumizil2005 Fig. 7). Calibration n is 5,000 on three datasets and 1,351 on phoneme, so dataset and n are confounded. Addressed in part by sens-ncal (isotonic on 1,351 calibration rows everywhere). Phoneme also has smaller training (2,702) and test (1,351) splits, so sens-ncal separates calibration n only, not training size or test noise; the paper attributes nothing to the dataset itself.

Electricity (OpenML 151) is a time series; random splits put neighbouring half-hours on both sides, which can make test predictions sharper and better calibrated than on future data and raises the correlation across seeds. The verdicts are scoped to these samples, so this is a scope and disclosure issue: stated here and in the paper's limitations, and measured by sens-elec-time (chronological split by file row order, which is the time order; the date column is not monotone and is not used), which is descriptive and not counted in the k-of-4 rule.

Electricity's Victoria columns (vicprice, vicdemand, transfer) hold constant fill values over the first 17,424 rows (about 38% of the file, 363 days), not measurements. Kept as distributed, they act as a regime indicator in the random splits, where filled and measured rows are mixed on both sides. In sens-elec-time the chronological train half (about the first 22,700 file rows) contains all filled rows while calibration and test contain none, so that sensitivity confounds temporal drift with the fill regime. Disclosed here and in the limitations; the share of filled rows in each split is recorded per seed; the columns are not imputed or dropped, so the data match those used by other studies.

Overlapping subsamples: two 20,000-row draws from about 45,000 rows share about 44% of rows, and phoneme reuses all rows, so the paired t(9) interval measures variability over resplits of these samples, not population sampling variance. Addressed by scoping every verdict to these samples (as the hypotheses state); no population claim is made.

'Library defaults' is a choice: tuned models (C, leaf size) calibrate differently (sources/notes.md D7), and default RF (min_samples_leaf=1) produces many 0/1 probabilities. The results apply to scikit-learn 1.9.1 defaults only. Departures are stated: LR max_iter=1000 (convergence recorded), HGB early_stopping=False (identical to 'auto' at these training sizes), shared one-hot encoding (HGB's native categorical handling unused).

Platt on the logit of the clipped probability: RF's exact 0/1 outputs become leverage points at about +/-13.8, which may distort the Platt fit for RF. Platt is descriptive only; its clip counts are reported.

Log-loss depends on the clipping epsilon when RF or isotonic output exact 0/1. Log-loss is descriptive; it is reported at eps 1e-6 with clip counts and at machine epsilon as a sensitivity, so readers can see how much of any difference the epsilon makes.
Isotonic regression introduces ties and can lower AUC, so a Brier change might come from lost discrimination. Addressed by reporting AUC for every cell (describe).

bank-marketing's call-duration feature is known only after the call (target leakage for deployment). It raises discrimination for all models alike and does not bias the within-model isotonic-versus-none comparison, but it is disclosed and the dataset's results are not read as deployment-realistic.

Three hypotheses on four datasets with unadjusted 95% intervals: some per-dataset categories could arise by chance. The k-of-4 overall rule was fixed at the question gate and no other comparison is confirmatory; this is stated in the paper.

Data version or metric-implementation errors. Addressed by the pinned manifest (row counts checked against OpenML metadata before analysis), unit-tests, the code review before any analysis run, single-threaded workers with fixed random_state, and the clean rerun at 1e-6 relative tolerance.

disclosures: 2026-11-19 (design stage, before any run on study data): After the question gate, H1's text was amended at the PI's ruling on design review design-r1 F1. It now names the plug-in 15-bin equal-mass ECE estimator as the measured quantity and states its bias direction (upward; near its noise floor for a well-calibrated model and shrinking toward zero for a miscalibrated one, so that RF minus LR is pulled toward zero when RF is the miscalibrated model), and that the debiased estimator of Kumar et al. (2019, Appendix G, Def. G.3) is reported beside it without changing the verdict. The confirmatory metric, margin (0.005), decision rule and comparison are unchanged; the claim is narrowed from calibration error to this estimator on these samples. The human sees this amendment at the design gate. The design-stage sensitivity that subtracted a simulated perfect-calibration floor (ece_adj) was replaced by the Kumar et al. estimator before any run.

2026-11-19: After the question gate, H1's label and the contribution were reworded at the Reviewer's request (design-r2 F5) from 'replication' to a test of the published direction on the plug-in estimator, because the two models' estimator noise floors alone could decide H1. The metric, margin and decision rule are unchanged. The human sees this at the design gate.

2026-11-19 (after the design gate, before any analysis run): At the PI's ruling on code review code-r1 F2 and F3, plan text was narrowed without changing any metric, margin, decision rule or code. (1) design.method step 8 and design.threats[0] now say that the Kumar et al. (2019) Def. G.3 debiased ECE removes only about 41% (2 - sqrt(2) of the floor remains, under the normal approximation) of a well-calibrated bin's l1 floor, not about all of it as the approved design said. (2) The replication licence was dropped: hypotheses[0]'s label and the contribution no longer say H1 is 'called a replication where the debiased ECE agrees in direction'; H1 is never called a replication, it is a test of the published direction on the plug-in estimator, and ece_db is reported descriptively. (3) design.method step 7 now says isotonic on the logit equals isotonic on the clipped probability only at the calibration points, with linear interpolation in the logit between them. H1's metric (plug-in 15-bin equal-mass ECE), margin (0.005) and decision rule are unchanged. This is a post-design-gate narrowing; the human sees it at the results gate.
